Descriptive Statistics Tables

Source: vignettes/articles/descriptives.qmd 
library(apa7)
library(flextable)
library(ftExtra)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(forcats)
library(stringr)
apa7_defaults(font_family = "Open Sans", line_spacing = 1.5)

Automatic Summaries with the apa_descriptives Function

The first table of most empirical papers describes the sample. apa_descriptives makes this table: for each continuous variable, its mean and standard deviation, M (SD), and for each categorical variable, the number and percentage of respondents at each level, n (%). Numeric variables are treated as continuous, and factors, character vectors, and logical vectors as categorical. Each categorical variable has a heading row, with its levels indented below it.

Data Set Summaries

The survey data set in the MASS package (Ripley & Venables, 2009) has the answers of 237 statistics students to a short questionnaire. Without groups, there is one column for the whole sample:

d_survey <- MASS::survey |>
  mutate(
    Exer = fct_recode(
      Exer, 
      Frequently = "Freq") |> 
      fct_relevel("Frequently", after = Inf),
    Smoke = fct_recode(
      Smoke, 
      Occasionally = "Occas", 
      Regularly = "Regul") |> 
      fct_relevel("Heavy", after = Inf)
  ) |> 
  select(Age, 
         `Height (cm)` = Height, 
         `Pulse (beats per minute)` = Pulse, 
         Smoking = Smoke, 
         Exercise = Exer,
         Sex)


apa_descriptives(d_survey, format_variable_names = FALSE) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Note. Values are M (SD) for continuous variables and n (%) for categorical variables. Percentages are of nonmissing responses. Missing values: 28 for Height (cm), 45 for Pulse (beats per minute), 1 for Smoking, and 1 for Sex.

Variables are named by their formatted names unless labels gives better ones. Percentages are of the non-missing responses, and the note lists the number of missing values of each variable that has any.

Groups

With by, each group gets a column, with its size in the header, followed by a column for the whole sample (total = FALSE leaves it out). Rows whose group is missing are left out, and the note says how many.

apa_descriptives(
  d_survey,
  format_variable_names = FALSE,
  by = Sex
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Skewed Variables and Group Differences

Age is strongly skewed in this sample (most students are about 20, a few much older), so its median and interquartile range, Mdn (IQR), describe it better. continuous sets the description of particular variables.

With test = "auto", a p column tests the group differences: Welch’s t test (two groups) or Welch’s one-way ANOVA (more groups) for variables described by their mean, the Kruskal–Wallis test for variables described by their median, and the chi-square test of independence for categorical variables. When a categorical variable’s table has an expected count below 5, where the chi-square approximation is poor, Fisher’s exact test is used for that variable instead, and the note names it (test = "chisq" or test = "fisher" uses one test for all categorical variables). Tests are not shown by default, because many journals discourage testing baseline differences in randomized trials, where any difference is due to chance.

apa_descriptives(
  d_survey,
  by = Sex,
  continuous = c(Age = "median_iqr"),
  test = "auto",
  format_variable_names = FALSE
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Missing Values and Ranges

By default, the note lists the missing values. With missing = "row", each variable with missing values gets a “Missing” row with the number of missing values in each column instead. With range = TRUE, each continuous variable gets a “Range” row with its minimum and maximum:

apa_descriptives(
  d_survey,
  by = Sex,
  missing = "row",
  format_variable_names = FALSE
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Options

  • categorical treats numeric codes (e.g., 1 = yes, 0 = no) as categories.
  • digits and percent_digits set the decimal places of the statistics and the percentages.
  • format_variable_names = FALSE keeps unlabeled variable names exactly as they are.

For tables with other layouts, see Building tables by hand, which shows how to make any data frame into an APA-style table.

References

Ripley, B., & Venables, B. (2009). MASS: Support functions and datasets for Venables and Ripley’s MASS (pp. 7.3–66). Comprehensive R Archive Network. https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.MASS
